To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a sequence learning OCR system trained on individual isolated characters is able to achieve state-of-the-art results on historical documents; and 2) a segmentation-free OCR system trained on semi-corrected text lines is able to achieve comparable performance to a segmentation-based OCR system.
we propose an iterative training approach for OCR, where the initial training data is a collection of scanned pages, and the final output is the corrected text.
we have presented a novel iterative framework to train an OCR system using minimal information, and have demonstrated its effectiveness by applying it to a collection of historical documents.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a novel iterative training framework for OCR, which is applicable for both historical documents as well as for present day documents, where manually transcribing training data is a laborious process.
the development of an OCR framework for historical documents which does not require any transcribed data.
the following questions: How to use the available information in the scanned documents to obtain satisfactory results?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the proposed iterative training procedure, starting from a segmentation-based OCR system and using a segmentation-free OCR system, is a viable approach for recognizing documents with limited training data.
our method is able to improve the accuracy of segmentation based methods, and is able to achieve a reasonable level of accuracy even with minimal training data.
our approach is able to achieve a high accuracy in recognizing text from historical documents, without the requirement of manually transcribed training documents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the proposed approach can be applied to any language and any historical documents, where transcribed training data may be scarce or non-existent.
the proposed framework can be used to digitize historical documents without the need for manual transcriptions.
we are able to obtain a character error rate (CER) of 6.8% on 15th century handwritten Latin manuscripts using only the minimal available training data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the proposed framework is not restricted to a specific language and can be applied to any language with the availability of a limited number of ground-truth documents.
the proposed iterative training framework can be applied in any scenario, where transcribed training data are not available, and can be used to improve the performance of OCR on historical documents.
a generic OCR framework, starting from the minimal amount of information available, can be used to digitize old documents.
